passage:
Ashtami, 11 pm
Feet are dead. Worth it.
Morning: Dadi woke us at five for the puja. I did the aarti plate this year for the first time! Didn't drop a single diya. Dadi said I held it 'just like your Dada used to'. I don't really know what all the Sanskrit means, but I know every word by heart, same as everyone.
Evening: kanya puja at Sharma Aunty's, then garba till the uncles begged for mercy. Vishal and I won the dandiya round, obviously.
I love how for these nine days the whole lane feels like one family. Nobody asks why we do it. We just do it, together, like every year.
Rajni
PS: tomorrow = halwa-puri 😋

qa.a: Dadi could share what the Sanskrit words mean and the stories behind them, so the warm belonging can grow along with understanding.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel watching Rajni hold the aarti plate?
qa.a: Dadi probably feels proud and moved, seeing Rajni carry a practice that Dada once did 🤍

grounding: It shows a teenager taking part in festival prayers as a warm, unquestioned part of family and neighbourhood life.

passage:
Nitin, you asked what Chhath is like. Okay, imagine this. Four in the morning, still dark, and our whole mohalla is walking to the river in Patna. Dadi carries the bamboo basket on her head, full of thekua and bananas and sugarcane. I carry the diya and try not to let it go out.
At the ghat the water is freezing. Dadi and Mummy stand in it up to their waists, facing east, and we all wait for the sun. Everybody sings the same songs I've heard since I was a baby. When the sun finally comes up, orange, everyone offers arghya together, and I get goosebumps every single time.
I don't really think about why we do it. It's just ours. It's Dadi's hand on my head afterwards, and thekua that tastes better than anything, and all my cousins in one place.
I'm Ganga, by the way, named after a river. So I suppose I was always going to love this festival.

qa.q: What does Dadi carry in the bamboo basket?
qa.a: Thekua and bananas and sugarcane.

qa.q: What does Ganga feel when the sun rises?
qa.a: Ganga feels awe and warm belonging, getting goosebumps every single time.

qa.q: What might Ganga gain by asking Dadi about the songs one day?
qa.a: Ganga could learn their meaning, deepening a warm tradition by understanding it and not only following it.

qa.q: What might Nitin feel hearing this description?
qa.a: Nitin likely feels curious and warmly included, getting a vivid picture of a festival that belongs to Ganga's family.

grounding: A teen describes a family festival as warm, unquestioned and woven into belonging, with no questions asked about why.

passage:
Three days before Losar. Pema helped her grandmother fold white khadas and polish the brass bowls for the altar. Ama-la showed her how to fill seven bowls with water, left to right, without spilling a drop. Pema didn't ask why seven. It was simply how it had always been.
Losar eve. The whole family climbed to the monastery above Gangtok. Pema spun the prayer wheels on the way up, one after another, the way her father had shown her when she was small. Inside, the monks chanted, butter lamps flickered, and she sat squeezed between her cousins, sleepy and happy.
Losar day. Rashmi from her class came over for the first time. Pema proudly showed her the altar and handed her khapse, the fried sweet biscuits. "What do the bowls mean?" Rashmi asked.
Pema opened her mouth, then laughed. "Honestly? I don't know. We just do it. It's home."

qa.q: How many water bowls did Pema fill?
qa.a: Seven bowls.

qa.q: What does Pema's laugh at Rashmi's question reveal?
qa.a: Pema feels warm and secure in the tradition, surprised to realise she has never questioned it because it simply feels like home.

qa.q: What could Pema do after Rashmi's question?
qa.a: Ask Ama-la what the seven bowls mean, keeping the warmth while learning the reasons.

qa.q: What might Rashmi feel visiting on Losar?
qa.a: Rashmi likely feels welcomed and curious, enjoying the sweets and the new customs.

grounding: Over the days of a festival a teen takes part in family rituals that feel warm, unquestioned and tied to belonging.

passage:
Simran, you asked why I still keep this tulsi mala in my pocket. Let me tell you about me at fourteen.
Every year, in the rains, my father and I walked with the wari to Pandharpur. Eighteen days on foot, with thousands of pilgrims singing abhangs, drums and cymbals, dust and mud. I didn't wonder whether Vitthal was listening. I didn't wonder anything. My feet hurt, my father's hand was on my shoulder, and an old woman from the next village fed me bhakri every evening as if I were her own grandson.
When we finally saw the temple spire, everyone wept and danced, and I did too, without knowing why. It was the happiest I have ever been.
Faith, for me then, was that crowd, my father's voice singing beside me, and that old woman's bhakri. That is what I still carry. I'm Nilesh; the questions came later, but that belonging never left.

qa.q: How many days did the walk to Pandharpur take?
qa.a: Eighteen days on foot.

qa.q: What did young Nilesh feel when the temple spire came into view?
qa.a: He felt overwhelming joy and belonging, weeping and dancing without needing to know why.

qa.q: What choice inside the story shaped Nilesh's faith?
qa.a: His father's choice to take him on the wari every year, which tied faith to walking together, singing and being fed by strangers.

qa.q: How might the old woman who fed Nilesh have seen him?
qa.a: She probably saw him as a young pilgrim to care for like her own grandson, sharing her bhakri out of kindness and devotion.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage pilgrimage where faith was warm, unquestioned and bound up with family and community belonging.

passage: The rain began before dawn on Eid, and by six the lane outside Rehana's house in Lucknow was ankle-deep. Abbu's train from Kanpur was running three hours late, and Ammi was worried he'd miss the namaz. Rehana didn't think about whether to pray; she simply tied her dupatta, helped her little sister with hers, and stirred the sheer khurma while Ammi wrapped the gifts. When the call to prayer sounded, faint through the rain, something in her chest settled, the way it did every year. Eshaan from next door arrived dripping, as he had every Eid since they were five, for his bowl. "Same taste as last year," he said, which from him was high praise. At ten, Abbu walked in soaked, laughing, and the whole family hugged him at once. Rehana felt, as always, that everything was exactly where it belonged.

qa.q: How late was Abbu's train from Kanpur running?
qa.a: Abbu's train from Kanpur was running three hours late.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel when the call to prayer sounds?
qa.a: Rehana feels calm and settled, a warm, familiar comfort that comes every year without any question.

qa.q: What might help Rehana later, if questions ever come?
qa.a: Knowing that her family's warmth and her own belonging are real could help her talk openly with Ammi or Abbu rather than feel alone with new questions.

qa.q: How does Eshaan experience Eid at Rehana's house?
qa.a: For Eshaan it is a happy yearly tradition, coming for his bowl of sheer khurma, and he feels part of the neighbourhood's celebration too.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking part in prayers and festival rituals as a warm, unquestioned part of family and community life.
